title: operator-bridge-script-and-legal-safe-phrasing-2026
author: Maya Thompson
body:
Summary:
This page provides an operator-facing bridge script, customer-facing status templates, and a short guidance matrix for legal-safe phrasing. It is intended for front-line bridge operators, on-call engineers, and SRE leads who must rapidly compose accurate, compliant customer notifications while minimizing legal exposure.

Who should use this document:
- Bridge operators (primary)
- On-call engineers and responders
- Customer Success for coordinated notices
- Legal for template review and approval

Objectives:
1) Give operators a single-sheet script to run the first 10–30 minutes of an incident.
2) Provide pre-approved, graded status messages for email, status page, and Slack with legal-safe phrasing.
3) Offer a short decision matrix for when to escalate to legal or account teams.

Section A — Quick operator bridge script (first 10 minutes):
1. Acknowledge and gather evidence (0–2 min)
   - Open the incident channel and set the bridge title: [SERVICE] Degraded / [REGION] Impact (e.g., embed-service-us-west - degraded).
   - Confirm severity using the SLO/impact rubric below.
   - Capture 3 core evidence points: number of failing requests, error rate, and first observed timestamp.
   - Short CLI snippets: `kubectl get pods -n inference -o wide` and `curl -sS https://monitoring.internal/api/v1/alerts?id=<alert-id>`
2. Stabilize and gather quick mitigations (2–8 min)
   - If throttling/backpressure: apply emergency rate-limit lift for critical tenant(s) only (runbook id: throttle-emergency-2024).
   - If model KV-cache saturation: trigger cache-eviction job (job id: kv-cache-evict) and monitor latency for 2 sequential minutes.
   - If instance crashloop: remove node from rollout pool and scale replacement nodes with autoscaler command.
3. Communicate (5–10 min)
   - Post an initial customer-facing status (Immediate Notice template A, see Section B).
   - Tag the incident severity and link to the monitoring evidence.
   - Notify account owners for any customers with >5% of affected traffic.
4. Escalate as needed (10 min)
   - If impact >S1 (see table), call incident manager & legal if customer data could be exposed or compliance boundaries hit.
   - If unknown scope, add a dedicated investigator and request full request logs snapshot.

Section B — Graded customer-facing templates (legal-safe):
Notes on safe phrasing: avoid speculation, do not apologize for unknowns, and use evidence-based language. Replace bracketed tokens before publishing.

Template A — Initial acknowledgement (suitable for status page & quick email):
"We are investigating an issue affecting [SERVICE] in [REGION]. Our automated alerts indicate elevated error rates and increased latency for a subset of requests. We have engaged the on-call team and are actively diagnosing. We will post an update within 30 minutes or sooner if the impact changes."

Template B — Follow-up update (after mitigations are in progress):
"Mitigation steps are in progress: we have implemented [mitigation action] and are observing [metric change]. Traffic is partially restored for some customers; however, residual errors continue for a subset of requests. We are continuing diagnostics and will provide the next update within 60 minutes."

Template C — Customer-impact summary (post-stabilization):
"Root cause analysis is ongoing. The incident caused elevated error rates for requests matching [signature] between [start timestamp] and [end timestamp]. We have restored normal service for the majority of traffic. We will share a post-incident report with a timeline and corrective actions within 72 hours."

Template D — High-sensitivity/legal notice (when to use):
Use only after consulting Legal/Compliance and INCIDENT_MANAGER. This language avoids admissions of liability and focuses on facts:
"Our investigation indicates that requests processed during [window] may have included identifiers for a limited set of customers. We are continuing a targeted forensic review and will notify impacted customers directly with recommended next steps. If you believe your data may be affected, please contact security@redwood.ai."

Section C — Severity & escalation matrix (short):
| Severity | Customer impact rule | Bridge actions | Legal? | Account notice? |
| S0 (Sev 0) | Total outage for >25% of regional traffic or SLA breach projected | Full bridge, exec notif, legal consult | Yes | Yes (exec) |
| S1 | Partial outage affecting >5% of customers or sustained latency >2x SLO | Full bridge, mitigation sprint | Maybe (if PII) | Yes |
| S2 | Single-customer outage or <5% multi-tenant impact | On-call bridge, targeted mitigation | No | Yes (affected accounts) |
| S3 | Noise, transient errors within acceptable SLO | Monitor, no customer notice required | No | No |

Section D — When to involve Legal: decision checklist
- Any evidence of data exposure, exfiltration, or non-trivial access to user data.
- Requests for customer-specific remediation or credits beyond standard SLAs.
- Regulatory scope (GDPR/CCPA/PCI) applies to potentially affected tenants.
- Statements that include cause, root-cause, or financial impact beyond high-level facts.
If any are true: ping legal@redwood.ai and include the incident timeline + logs snapshot.

Section E — Operator scripts for different channels (examples)
1) Slack short notice (public #status channel):
"STATUS: [SERVICE] - Investigating increased errors in [REGION]. On-call is engaged. Initial evidence: [X% error, avg latency Yms]. Update in 30m."
2) Email to affected account owners (private):
Subject: [Redwood] Incident affecting [SERVICE] in [REGION] — initial notice
Body: [Template A with account-specific note and contact for updates]
3) Status page / RSS: use Template A then Template B/C as progress continues. Always include UTC timestamps and link to the incident ticket.

Section F — Post-incident artifacts to create (first 72 hours):
- Postmortem draft using the standard postmortem template (link to PM template).
- Timeline with evidence (logs, traces) exported as attachments.
- Corrective action list (owners, due dates) and a regression test plan for the change that caused the incident.
- Customer impact spreadsheet for account outreach.

Section G — On-call rotation & communication coordination notes
- Primary bridge operator responsibilities: start/close bridge, own the status messages, coordinate mitigations.
- Secondary (investigator): owns deep-dive diagnostics and log collection.
- Communication lead: owns customer notices and liaises with CS & legal.
- Rotation guidance: primary bridge shifts should be no longer than 12 hours for live rotations, with 1-hour stagger between handoffs.

Section H — Game day scenario (30–60 minute exercise):
Objective: validate legal-safe messaging + account notification flow for a partial multi-tenant outage.
Pre-reqs: sandbox status page, synthetic traffic generator, two volunteer account owners.
Exercise flow:
1) Trigger synthetic error spike for model-serving in us-east-1.
2) Operator executes bridge script and posts Initial A.
3) Investigator collects logs and attempts mitigation.
4) Communication lead crafts final customer-impact summary using Template C and routes to account owners.
5) After action: measure time to first customer notice, time to mitigations, and number of legal consults.
Success criteria: first public notice <10 minutes; mitigation applied <25 minutes; legal engaged only when checklist true.

Appendix — Quick reference snippets and common phrasing rules:
- Avoid: "We caused" / "We leaked" / "Customer data was accessed" until forensics complete.
- Prefer: "We observed" / "Our investigation indicates" / "We are conducting a targeted review".
- Time formatting: always use ISO 8601 UTC timestamps (2026-02-03T15:04:05Z).
- Contact list: incident_manager@redwood.ai, legal@redwood.ai, security@redwood.ai, cs-oncall@redwood.ai.

Ownership and maintenance:
Owner: SRE Bridge Team (team-slack: #bridge-ops). Please route template change requests through the runbook governance process. Legal must review any changes to Template D or messages that could be construed as root-cause statements.
